paragraphs.source_en: Mr. Harisaku of the previous letter signed himself Nine Bows, whereas this fellow offers only Two Bows; since he is not asking for donations, he puts on about seven bows' worth of airs. Though it is not a request for donations, it is instead exceedingly hard to understand. I thought that if such stuff were submitted to any magazine, it would certainly be rejected, and that my master, famous for the opacity of his brain, would surely tear it into strips and throw it away; but not at all, he turned it over and over and read it again and again. Perhaps he believed there was some profound meaning in a letter like this and had resolved to get to the bottom of it. Generally speaking, there are many things between heaven and earth that cannot be understood, yet if you set out to attach some meaning to them, there is nothing to which it cannot be done. No matter how difficult a piece of writing may be, if one wishes to interpret it, an interpretation can be supplied without much trouble. Whether you say man is foolish or man is clever, the matter is easily understood. Nor is that all: to say that man is a dog or a pig is not a proposition over which one need suffer greatly. Say that mountains are low, and there is no harm in it; say that the universe is narrow, and that too presents no difficulty. Even if one says crows are white, Ono no Komachi was an ugly woman, and Mr. Kushami is a gentleman, it is not necessarily impossible to make it pass. Thus, even a meaningless letter like this can be made to yield some meaning if only one fastens one argument or another onto it. Especially a man like my master, who has always forced explanations onto English he does not know, is all the more eager to attach meaning to such a composition. A student once asked him why one says Good morning even when the weather is plainly bad. He thought about that for a full seven days; and when someone asked what the English name Columbus was in Japanese, he spent three days and nights devising an answer. For such a man, whether vinegared dried gourd be a man of the realm, or whether eating Korean ginseng may raise a revolution, arbitrary meanings will naturally spring up everywhere. After a while, the master seemed to have swallowed these difficult phrases by his Good morning method and said, This is very deep in meaning; it must be by someone who has studied philosophy considerably, a truly admirable insight! So saying, he went on praising it extravagantly. From that single remark one can see quite well how foolish my master is. Yet, if one turns the matter over, there may be a little justice in it. My master has the habit of venerating anything whatever that he cannot understand. This can hardly be said to be my master's habit alone; where something is not understood, there seems to lurk within it something not to be made light of, and around the unfathomable there easily arises a feeling that it is somehow lofty. For that reason, ordinary people like to advertise things they do not understand as though they understood them. Scholars, on the other hand, explain things that are understandable in such a way that no one can understand them. Take university professors: everyone knows that those who lecture on things no one understands enjoy a high reputation; whereas those who explain things everyone can understand have little public esteem.

paragraphs.source_zh: 前一封信的针作先生是九拜，而这个家伙只是再拜，由于不是来募捐就蛮横地摆起架子，免了七拜。虽然不来募捐，不过却很难让人读懂。我想这种东西不管向哪家杂志投稿，都保证不会被采用的，所以我认为头脑不透明的主人肯定会把它撕得一条一条扔掉，然而满不是这么回事，他翻过来掉过去，读了又读。也许他认为这种信里边含有深意，决心把它的意义研究出来吧。说起来，天地之间弄不懂的东西多得很，不过你要给它加上某种意义，那么没有一件事是做不到的。不管多么艰深的文章，只要你想解释它，就可以不用太费力给予解释。你说人是愚蠢还是聪明，这是不必费劲儿就可明白的。还不只这样，说人是狗、是猪，也不是个很困难的命题。你说山是低的，没关系；你说宇宙是狭小的，也不妨事。你就是说乌鸦是白的，小野小町是丑八怪，苦沙弥先生是君子，也不见得不可以。所以像这种不知所云的信，如果硬给它这样那样的解释，那么也会找出点意义来。尤其是像主人这样，把不懂的英语牵强附会，硬要做出说明的人，就更想给这篇文章附上意义了。学生问他：“明明天气不好的时候，为什么还要说Good morning？”这使他足足思考了七天，有人问Columbus这个英文名字在日本话中怎么说，他费了三天三夜琢磨如何回答。所以对他这样的人，醋腌干瓢是天下之士也罢，吃朝鲜人参来发动革命也罢，当然随时都可以找出任意的解释的。过了一会儿，主人似乎用他那套解释Good morning的方法弄懂了这些难解的语句，说道：“这意义太深了，准是个对哲理有相当研究的人，真有极高的见识！”说着，不住地赞叹。从这一句话里也可以看出主人是如何的愚蠢。但如果反过来想，也可能有些对的地方。主人有个癖好，不管什么事凡是弄不懂的，都值得崇拜。这也很难说只是主人的癖好，既然不懂，其中必然潜伏着不可轻视的东西，在莫测高深之中，很容易诱发一种心理，认为好像是什么高贵得很。正因为如此，所以那些俗人总喜欢不懂装懂来给自己贴金。相反，学者则把本来可以懂的东西，解释得使人听不懂。就拿大学教授来说，大家都知道，那些专讲别人听不懂的课的人，总是声望很高的；而讲别人都能听懂的人，声望却不高。

paragraphs.source_en: The reason my master admired this letter was not that he had understood its meaning, but that it was almost impossible to grasp what its drift might be, because sea cucumber suddenly appeared in it and then suddenly the excrement of extremity appeared as well. Thus the sole reason my master respected this piece of writing is no different from the Taoists' reverence for the Tao Te Ching, the Confucians' reverence for the Book of Changes, or the Zen school's reverence for the Record of Linji: namely, that it is wholly incomprehensible. Still, being unable to understand it at all is unsatisfying, so one adds arbitrary annotations and at least assumes the look of someone who understands. To suppose one understands what one does not understand, and then to admire it, has been a delightful thing since ancient times. The master reverently rolled up this letter written in clerical script, placed it on the desk, folded his hands inside his sleeves, and sank into meditation.

units.source_zh: 因此，主人之所以尊敬这篇文章的唯一理由，正和道家尊敬《道德经》、儒家尊敬《易经》、禅家尊敬《临济录》没有什么两样，都是因为完全读不懂。

paragraphs.source_en: Just then, from the front door, someone called loudly into the house, Is anyone there? Is anyone there? The voice sounded like Meitei, yet, unlike Meitei, the visitor kept calling out properly to announce his presence. The master had heard the voice from his study for some time, but he remained with his hands tucked in his sleeves and did not move in the least. Perhaps he holds the principle that going out to receive callers is not the master's business; at any rate, this master never once answers from his study. The maid, Osan, had gone out to buy laundry soap, and the mistress was in the privy. That left only me to go to the entrance and receive the guest, but I had no desire to go either. Thereupon the guest sprang from the place for removing shoes up onto the raised floor, slid open the shoji, and strode straight into the house. The master is odd enough, but the guest is odd enough too. The visitor seems first to have gone toward the parlor; the sliding doors there opened and shut several times, and then he came toward the study. It was indeed Meitei.
